policy: Private research display only. No canonical relationship, identity, publication, family, tier, destination or physical-move writes. Context nodes never imply museum holdings.

sections.title: Datta Tradition
context: The Datta tradition reveres Narasimha Saraswati and Swami Samarth of Akkalkot as manifestations of Dattatreya. Sripada Srivallabha belongs to this traditional incarnation story too; his grey box supplies context without claiming a relic placement. These are incarnation connections, distinct from the teacher–disciple links below.
Balappa and Krishna Saraswati of Kolhapur are identified as Akkalkot Maharaj’s disciples. Placing the three together makes this personal teaching relationship visible.
placementSuggestions: Give Dattatreya, Narasimha Saraswati and Akkalkot a clear central grouping in Vitrine 1. A label can explain their traditional incarnation connection.
Keep Balappa and Krishna Saraswati close to Akkalkot in Vitrine 1, as two disciples beside their teacher.

sections.title: Maharashtra Guru Lineages
context: Meher Baba credited these masters with his spiritual unfolding, especially Babajan and Upasani. Sai Baba also links directly to Upasani. This arrangement makes several relationships visible at once.
Godavari Mata was Upasani’s disciple and succeeded him at Sakori. She belongs close to Upasani within this cluster; she is not one of Meher Baba’s Five Perfect Masters.
placementSuggestions: Use Meher Baba as the centre, with Hazrat Babajan and Upasani Maharaj close on either side. Place Shirdi Sai Baba next to Upasani, and Tajuddin Baba on another side of the Meher cluster.
Place Godavari Mata beside Upasani in Vitrine 2. Her proposed move from Vitrine 9 has been saved and verified.

sections.title: Samarth Ramdas and Venabai
context: Venabai was a disciple of Samarth Ramdas and a poet within his tradition. Her presence makes the teaching community around Ramdas visible.
placementSuggestions: Place Venabai beside Ramdas in Vitrine 9, with her disciple relationship identified on the label. Both are already proposed in this vitrine.

sections.title: Gajanan Maharaj and Bhaskar
context: The Shegaon institution recounts how Bhaskar Patil met Gajanan Maharaj at Adgaon and then accompanied him to Shegaon. This gives the smaller Bhaskar display a clear personal connection to Gajanan.
placementSuggestions: Keep Bhaskar next to Gajanan in Vitrine 9. A short label can identify him as Bhaskar Patil and refer to their Adgaon–Shegaon story.

sections.title: Bhagavan Nityananda’s circle
context: Shaligram Swami, also known as Dayananda, closely attended Bhagavan Nityananda. The lineage archive also identifies Balyogi Sadanand of Tungareshwar/Ganeshpuri as a disciple; he is distinct from Sadananda of Kanhangad.
placementSuggestions: Keep Shaligram close to Nityananda, with Balyogi Sadanand as a separate branch rather than a successor to Shaligram. All three are already proposed in Vitrine 10.

sections.title: Sivananda and Chinmayananda
context: Sivananda gave Chinmayananda sannyasa and then sent him to Tapovan Maharaj for Vedanta study. Chinmayananda’s story therefore connects two teachers with different roles.
placementSuggestions: Keep Chinmayananda beside or just after Sivananda in Vitrine 3. A short label can explain the initiation and subsequent study with Tapovan; the grey Tapovan box is context only.

sections.title: Haidakhan Babaji and Mahendra Baba
context: The Haidakhan tradition remembers Mahendra Baba as a devotee who foretold Babaji’s later appearance. The museum biography also connects Mahendra with Haidakhan visions. This is a devotional connection across generations, rather than an ordinary direct-disciple chain.
placementSuggestions: Keep Mahendra beside Haidakhan Babaji in Vitrine 3. A label can explain his role in preparing devotees for Babaji’s appearance; use an association line rather than a guru–disciple arrow.

sections.title: Himalayan lineages and Kashi
context: Yogananda describes Lahiri and Trailanga as friends who meditated together in Benares. Their positions can connect the Kriya and Kashi displays through a personal relationship visitors would otherwise miss.
Daya Mata, Durga Mata and Kriyananda were Yogananda’s direct disciples. Show them as branches beside him, rather than as successive gurus.

Karar Ashram names Hariharananda and Motilal Mukherjee among Yukteswar’s pupils. Show them as parallel branches. Hariharananda also learned from other teachers; this diagram shows one part of his training.
placementSuggestions: Read the Kriya group in this order: Lahiri Mahasaya, Sri Yukteswar, then Paramahansa Yogananda. Place each beside the next. Keep Daya Mata, Durga Mata and Kriyananda close to Yogananda. Keep Hariharananda and Motilal near Yukteswar, alongside the Yogananda branch.
Put the Lahiri end of the Kriya sequence toward neighbouring Vitrine 5. Place Trailanga Swami toward Vitrine 4 in the Kashi display.

sections.title: Sikh Gurus
context: The Sikh Gurus form a succession of Guruship. This gives a clear order for the five Gurus currently represented here, while the intervening grey boxes explain the gaps in that sequence. It is not a biological family tree.
placementSuggestions: Within Vitrine 11, read the represented Gurus in this order: Nanak, Amar Das, Arjan, Hargobind, then Gobind Singh. Use their Guru numbers on labels so the gaps are clear. Keep other saints beside this sequence without inserting them into the succession.
Work around the fixed relic in Vitrine 11; this is an order for the movable displays, not an instruction to move the fixed object.

sections.title: Varkari
context: Janabai’s life and devotional poetry are closely connected with Namdev and his household. Keeping the two names together makes that personal context visible.
placementSuggestions: Place Janabai directly beside Namdev in the Varkari display.

sections.title: Mahaprabhu and the early Gaudiya circle
context: Mahaprabhu’s circle brings together different relationships: Vishnupriya was his wife, Haridas a close devotional associate, and Sarvabhauma a Puri scholar who became his devotee. Chand Kazi belongs to the Navadwip story of dialogue and reconciliation.

Gopala Bhatta and Jiva belong to the Six Goswamis of Vrindavan. Keep this early circle distinct from the much later Gaudiya Math branches. Grey boxes supply wider context without claiming another relic placement.
placementSuggestions: Make Mahaprabhu the centre of this group in Vitrine 19, with Vishnupriya and Haridas close by. Keep Gopala Bhatta and Jiva together as part of the Goswami circle.
Place Sarvabhauma toward the Puri-facing side, connecting Mahaprabhu’s story with Vitrine 20. Put Chand Kazi toward the Vitrine 19 side of Vitrine 18, with a label connecting his story to Mahaprabhu.

sections.title: Gaudiya Math and the Radharaman branch
context: Gaura Kishor belongs on the teacher side; the other three were Bhaktisiddhanta’s disciples. A small branching arrangement makes their shared source and distinct later missions clear.
Lalita was Radharaman’s disciple and biographer. The close relationship is worth making visible within this large Gaudiya grouping.
placementSuggestions: Keep Gaura Kishor Das Babaji beside Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati. Arrange A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Bhakti Pramod Puri and Bhakti Prajnana Keshav as neighbouring branches around Bhaktisiddhanta.
Place Lalita Sakhi beside Radharaman Charan Das in Vitrine 18. Both are now planned together in this vitrine.

sections.title: Jagadbandhu and the Mahanam circle
context: Mahanambrata’s institutional biography names Mahendra Brahmachari as the guru who initiated him. Jagadbandhu is the central devotional figure of the Mahanam tradition. The missing intermediate generation matters when explaining this group.
placementSuggestions: Keep Mahanambrata near Jagadbandhu in Vitrine 18, with a label naming Mahendra as his initiating guru. Keep this as a recognisable cluster alongside the separate Radharaman–Lalita pair, rather than presenting the whole vitrine as one direct disciple chain.

sections.title: Jagannath Puri and Odisha
context: Kuladananda was his close disciple and attendant. His diary preserves the teacher’s conversations, giving this pair a clear teacher-and-recorder story.
placementSuggestions: Place Kuladananda Brahmachari beside Vijay Krishna Goswami in Vitrine 20. Both are now planned together; the diary connection can be explained on a short label.

sections.title: Bengal Shakta Baul and Modern Saints
context: Mokshada Sundari was Ma’s mother and a spiritual figure in her own right. This is a biological family connection, distinct from a guru–disciple link.
placementSuggestions: Place Mokshada Sundari Devi beside Anandamayi Ma. Label her with the familiar name Didima as well, so the connection is easy to recognise.

sections.title: Bamakhepa and Nigamananda
context: Nigamananda’s tradition describes his tantric training under Bamakhepa at Tarapith, followed by sannyasa under Sachchidananda Saraswati. These are different teacher roles in one life.
placementSuggestions: Keep Nigamananda beside Bamakhepa in Vitrine 21. Label the connection as tantric training. The grey sannyasa-teacher box supplies context and does not identify a second museum holding.

sections.title: Dilip Kumar Roy and Indira Devi
context: Dilip Kumar Roy was a disciple of Sri Aurobindo. Indira Devi was Roy’s disciple, and together they established Hari Krishna Mandir in Pune. Their shared work makes a clear pair within the wider eastern grouping.
placementSuggestions: Place Indira beside Dilip Kumar Roy in Vitrine 22, keeping their Pune work visible as a pair. The grey Aurobindo box explains Roy’s earlier lineage context without claiming a relic placement.
